DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: ACTIV-6, an ongoing, decentralized, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled platform trial, was designed to evaluate repurposed therapies in outpatients with mild to moderate COVID-19. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Time to sustained recovery, defined as at least 3 consecutive days without symptoms. There were 7 secondary outcomes, including a composite of hospitalization or death by day 28. RESULTS: Among 1800 participants who were randomized (mean [SD] age, 48 [12] years; 932 women [58.6%]; 753 [47.3%] reported receiving at least 2 doses of a SARS-CoV-2 vaccine), 1591 completed the trial. The hazard ratio (HR) for improvement in time to recovery was 1.07 (95% credible interval [CrI], 0.96-1.17; posterior P value [HR >1] = .91). The median time to recovery was 12 days (IQR, 11-13) in the ivermectin group and 13 days (IQR, 12-14) in the placebo group. There were 10 hospitalizations or deaths in the ivermectin group and 9 in the placebo group (1.2% vs 1.2%; HR, 1.1 [95% CrI, 0.4-2.6]). The most common serious adverse events were COVID-19 pneumonia (ivermectin [n = 5]; placebo [n = 7]) and venous thromboembolism (ivermectin [n = 1]; placebo [n = 5]). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among outpatients with mild to moderate COVID-19, treatment with ivermectin, compared with placebo, did not significantly improve time to recovery. text:
I found ten large or well-designed randomized trials and the main systematic reviews. The higher-quality trials consistently find that ivermectin does not meaningfully help people with COVID-19, whether the outcome is recovery time, hospitalization, death or how fast the virus clears. Early meta-analyses reported large benefits, but those results depended on low-quality and possibly fraudulent studies. That makes this topic a good case study for a research methods course.

## 1. Key randomized controlled trials

### Outpatients with early or mild-to-moderate COVID-19

| Trial | Design / setting | N (IVM vs control) | Dose | Primary outcome | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **López-Medina et al., JAMA 2021** [W3135420706] | Double-blind, placebo-controlled; Cali, Colombia | 200 vs 200 | 300 µg/kg × 5 d | Time to symptom resolution | Median 10 vs 12 days; HR 1.07 (95% CI 0.87–1.32), P = .53 |
| **TOGETHER, NEJM 2022** [W4220754707] | Double-blind adaptive platform; 12 clinics in Brazil; patients at high risk | 679 vs 679 | 400 µg/kg × 3 d | COVID hospitalization or emergency department (ED) observation >6 h by day 28 | 14.7% vs 16.3%; RR 0.90 (95% CrI 0.70–1.16). Similar in modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses |
| **COVID-OUT, NEJM 2022** [W4292148078] | Double-blind, 2×3 factorial; US adults with overweight or obesity | 1,323 analyzed (all arms) | — | Low blood oxygen, ED visit, hospitalization or death | aOR 1.05 (95% CI 0.76–1.45) for ivermectin |
| **ACTIV-6 (400 µg/kg), JAMA 2022** [W4307043809] | Decentralized double-blind platform; 93 US sites | 817 vs 774 | 400 µg/kg × 3 d | Time to sustained recovery | HR 1.07 (95% CrI 0.96–1.17); hospitalization or death 1.2% vs 1.2% |
| **ACTIV-6 (600 µg/kg), JAMA 2023** [W4321369786] | Same platform; 83.5% vaccinated | 602 vs 604 | Up to 600 µg/kg × 6 d | Time to sustained recovery | Median 11 vs 11 days; HR 1.02 (95% CrI 0.92–1.13) |
| **PRINCIPLE, J Infect 2024** [W4392303143] | Open-label platform; UK community | 2,157 vs 3,256 usual care | 300–400 µg/kg × 3 d | Self-reported recovery; hospitalization or death | Recovery about 2 days faster (HR 1.15), but only 19% probability of reaching the pre-specified meaningful effect (HR ≥1.2). Hospitalization or death OR 1.02 (0.63–1.62). No difference at 3, 6 or 12 months |
| **I-TECH, JAMA Intern Med 2022** [W4212973150] | Open-label; 20 hospitals in Malaysia; age ≥50 with other health conditions | 241 vs 249 | 400 µg/kg × 5 d | Progression to severe disease (needing oxygen) | 21.6% vs 17.3%; RR 1.25 (0.87–1.80). Mortality RR 0.31 (0.09–1.11), not significant |

### Effect on the virus
- **PLATCOV, eLife 2023** [W4321366419]: an open-label randomized platform trial using a high dose (600 µg/kg × 7 days). The ivermectin arm was stopped for futility. Viral clearance was 9.1% *slower* than with no drug (95% CI −27.2% to +11.8%). In the same trial, a monoclonal antibody arm cleared the virus 52% faster, which shows the method could detect a real antiviral effect.

### Smaller trials to consider including
These need careful risk-of-bias assessment:
- Ivermectin vs. standard care in Thailand [W4313121933]
- CORVETTE-01 [W4377292376]
- Single- vs. double-dose ivermectin [W4283363264]
- IVERCOR-COVID19 [W3173645873]
- Hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 [W4220768079]
- Combination with doxycycline [W3162891398]

## 2. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses

**Cochrane living review (Popp et al., 2022)** [W4283205481]. This is the most rigorous synthesis I found. It only included trials that were registered *prospectively*, as an integrity filter, and this excluded 7 of the 14 trials from its previous version. It then included 11 RCTs (3,409 participants):
- **Outpatients:** ivermectin probably has little or no effect on 28-day death (RR 0.77, 0.47–1.25; moderate certainty) and no effect on quality of life (high certainty).
- **Inpatients:** the evidence is very low certainty. The authors remain uncertain about effects on death.
- **Prevention:** no eligible trials.
- **Conclusion:** for outpatients there is "low- to high-certainty evidence that ivermectin has no beneficial effect."

Note that its search ran to December 2021, plus large trials up to April 2022. It therefore predates COVID-OUT, both ACTIV-6 reports, PRINCIPLE and PLATCOV, all of which point the same way.

**Early positive meta-analyses:**
- **Bryant et al., Am J Ther 2021** [W3168908540]: pooled 15 trials and found a 62% reduction in deaths (RR 0.38, 0.19–0.73), rated "moderate certainty." Its reference list includes a pilot trial in *Toxicology Reports* [W3134585354] that was later **retracted** [10.1016/j.toxrep.2022.04.009]. It also includes several small or non-randomized studies.
- **Hill et al., OFID 2021** [W3121596699]: this meta-analysis was **retracted** [10.1093/ofid/ofac056].
- **Hill, Mirchandani & Pilkington, OFID 2022** [W4206432189]: these authors redid the analysis stratified by trial quality. The survival benefit "was dependent on largely poor-quality studies." The potentially fraudulent trial showed RR 0.08 (0.02–0.35), while trials at low risk of bias showed RR 0.96 (0.56–1.66), meaning no effect.

## 3. Why early and later evidence disagree
1. **Research integrity problems.** At least two ivermectin trials in this database have been retracted: the *Toxicology Reports* pilot [10.1016/j.toxrep.2022.04.009] and the IRICT trial [10.1080/14787210.2024.2362097]. The trial that Hill et al. 2022 call potentially fraudulent is widely reported to be the Elgazzar preprint, but I couldn't find that record in this database. Please check it against the Retraction Watch database before citing it.
2. **Small-study effects.** The large benefits come from small, often open-label, single-site trials. Large, multi-site, placebo-controlled trials (TOGETHER, ACTIV-6, COVID-OUT, PRINCIPLE) find effects close to zero.
3. **Weak biological basis.** Ivermectin only stopped the virus in lab studies at concentrations much higher than standard doses reach in the body (noted in [W3111068209] and [W3121596699]). Even very high doses showed no antiviral effect in PLATCOV [W4321366419].
4. **Possible confounding by parasitic infection.** This is a hypothesis from the wider literature, not something these trials tested. In places where *Strongyloides* worms are common, ivermectin might prevent worm-related deaths in patients given steroids, which could look like a COVID benefit [W4378516419].

## 4. Suggestions for your methods
- **Pre-specify an integrity screen**, for example Cochrane's rule of prospective trial registration only. Then run sensitivity analyses with and without trials at high risk of bias or under suspicion.
- **Check every included trial for retractions or expressions of concern.** Several ivermectin papers and one meta-analysis have been retracted.
- **Stratify by population** (outpatient, inpatient, prevention), because the certainty of evidence differs sharply between them.
- **Use GRADE.** The Cochrane review shows how to rate certainty for each outcome.
- **Distinguish statistical from clinical significance.** PRINCIPLE is a good teaching example: a statistically significant 2-day faster recovery, in an open-label trial with self-reported outcomes, that was unlikely to reach the pre-specified meaningful effect size.

## Bottom line
In large, well-run, mostly placebo-controlled randomized trials, ivermectin does not reduce hospitalization or death, does not meaningfully speed recovery, and does not speed viral clearance in COVID-19. This holds across doses (300–600 µg/kg), treatment lengths (3–7 days), countries, and vaccinated and unvaccinated groups. The apparent benefit in early meta-analyses disappears once low-quality and suspect trials are excluded.

I should have given you my criteria. Only randomized controlled trials of oral or intravenous ivermectin in people with confirmed or suspected COVID-19, compared with placebo, no treatment, standard care or another drug. No prophylaxis trials in people without COVID-19, no observational studies, no lab or animal studies, and no reviews. Please give me the full updated list of included trials.

{"id": "W4406827333", "doi": "10.3855/jidc.19862", "title": "Role of ivermectin and colchicine in the treatment of COVID-19: a randomized controlled clinical trial", "abstract": "INTRODUCTION: The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of ivermectin and colchicine as treatment options for coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). METHODOLOGY: A three-arm randomized controlled clinical trial was conducted in the Triage Clinic of the family medicine department at Ain Shams University Hospitals on participants who had been diagnosed with moderate COVID-19. Patients aged < 18 years or > 65 years, with any co-morbidities, pregnant or lactating females, and those with mild or severe COVID-19 confirmed cases were excluded. Sealed envelopes were used for randomization of intervention or control. Patients are followed until there was improvement of symptoms and no development of new symptoms for over one month. RESULTS: A total of 120 patients (40.16 ± 10.74 years) with COVID-19 were enrolled; 40 patients in each arm. Out of them, 44 (36.6%) were male and 76 (63.4%) were female. Fever and cough were the predominant symptoms in each group. There was no statistically significant difference in the mean duration of fever between the ivermectin, colchicine, and control groups (7.3 ± 1.68, 6.6 ± 1.58, and 7.075 ± 1.58 days, respectively). I found 48 records that look like eligible trials; they come to 49 trials once the two companion trials in one paper are split. I read the full abstract for 30 and judged the other 18 on title and snippet only, because I hit the tool-call limit before I could open them. Three more are retracted or withdrawn, and two have unclear randomization. Everything comes from one literature database, so this is not yet a complete systematic search.

**Correction to my last answer.** I said ivermectin "does not speed viral clearance." That holds for the larger trials (PLATCOV, COVER, Krolewiecki). But some trials on this list report the opposite. A double-blind trial in Sri Lanka [W4400881102] found a lower viral load at day 10 (per-protocol analysis, P=0.022) but no clinical benefit. Several small open-label trials also report faster PCR negativity [W3126179459, W4312323281, W3129242298]. Keep viral clearance as an outcome where the trials disagree.

- **Prophylaxis in people without COVID-19:**

- **Retracted or withdrawn.** Excluded: Pott-Junior [W3134585354], IRICT [W4283838215] and Elgazzar [W3110602237].

- **Niaee 2021, Iran** [W3111064783]: 180 patients. Four ivermectin arms vs hydroxychloroquine and hydroxychloroquine + placebo. Deaths were 0–10% with ivermectin vs 16.7–20% in the control arms. ## D. On hold until full-text review

- **Kishoria 2020** [W3088905160]: the title suggests ivermectin added to hydroxychloroquine, but the abstract has no methods or results.

## Synthesis

These are descriptive patterns from the abstracts, not a meta-analysis.

**Mortality**
- No trial found a statistically significant reduction in deaths.
- Several small hospital trials had point estimates favouring ivermectin, all with wide confidence intervals:
  - Heydari: 4.5% vs 11.8%
  - Ochoa-Jaramillo: 5.4% vs 10.5%
  - Abd-Elsalam: 3 vs 4 deaths
- I-TECH, the largest trial reporting deaths separately, also leaned towards ivermectin, but its interval crossed 1 (RR 0.31, 0.09–1.11).
- Rezai's 609-patient inpatient trial and the placebo-controlled Beltran Gonzalez and Manomaipiboon trials found no difference.
- Deaths were rare among outpatients, so the outpatient trials can't detect a mortality effect.
- Overall, the deaths evidence is imprecise and comes mostly from small, often open-label trials. That matches Cochrane's "very low certainty" rating for inpatient mortality [W4283205481].
- If you include Niaee, it will drive any pooled mortality benefit. Run a sensitivity analysis without it.

**Hospitalization and disease progression**
- This is the most consistent outcome, and it shows no effect.
- The large placebo-controlled outpatient trials are all close to no effect:
  - TOGETHER: RR 0.90 (0.70–1.16)
  - COVID-OUT: aOR 1.05
  - ACTIV-6: 1.2% vs 1.2%
- The mid-sized trials point in both directions, with confidence intervals crossing no effect:
  - favouring ivermectin: IVERCOR (OR 0.65), Mirahmadizadeh (−2.3% and −3.9%)
  - favouring control: Rezai outpatient (RR 1.36), I-TECH (progression RR 1.25)
- The only clearly positive result is Chahla, the cluster trial with the reporting inconsistencies.

**Symptom resolution**
- The large blinded trials with symptom resolution as their primary outcome are neutral:
  - López-Medina: HR 1.07 (0.87–1.32)
  - ACTIV-6: HR 1.07 (0.96–1.17), about one day difference in median recovery
- Angkasekwinai numerically favoured placebo (76% vs 82%).
- Several smaller trials found benefits on secondary or individual symptoms: Rezai outpatient (fever), Shahbaznejad (dyspnea and cough), Chaccour (sense of smell).
- These positive findings tend to come from trials that measured many outcomes, which makes chance findings more likely, and some were open-label or small.

**Overall**
- Trials at lower risk of bias (large, blinded, placebo-controlled, prospectively registered) consistently find no meaningful benefit on any of the three outcomes.
- Positive findings cluster in small, open-label or single-centre trials, and often on secondary outcomes.
- Your date cut-off removes several large neutral trials (PRINCIPLE, ACTIV-6 600 µg/kg, IVERMILCO). It doesn't change the direction of the evidence, but it does lower its precision.
- Many smaller trials report faster viral clearance, but that hasn't translated into clinical benefit.

## Limitations
- The search covered one database only, and I judged trials from abstracts.
- Some sample sizes and mortality figures aren't in the abstracts (Ravikirti, Saxena, López-Medina deaths), so you'll need the full texts for data extraction.
- I didn't check trial-registry entries. That's needed if you add a prospective-registration rule like Cochrane's.

It should have been included. Missing it was my error, not an eligibility decision. The paper is Okumuş et al. 2021, *BMC Infectious Diseases* [W3130646175], and it meets all your criteria.

**Why I missed it.** None of my keyword searches returned it. It did appear in the reference list of the Bryant meta-analysis [W3168908540], which I pulled in my first answer. **Eligibility check**
- **Randomized:** yes. The authors describe a prospective, randomized, single-blind phase 3 trial.
- **Population:** hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia.
- **Same other treatments in both arms:** yes. Both arms got hydroxychloroquine + favipiravir + azithromycin; the study arm also got ivermectin, 200 µg/kg/day for 5 days, given enterally. This is an add-on design.
- **Date and format:** journal article, published 2021.
- **Not retracted** in this database.

**Main findings**
- 66 patients randomized: 36 to ivermectin, 30 to control.
- Clinical improvement at the end of 5 days of follow-up: 73.3% (22/30) vs 53.3% (16/30), P = 0.10.
- Deaths: 20% (6/30) vs 30% (9/30), P = 0.37.
